subject: PHS
vignette: An 80-year-old man with advanced dementia is hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia. He has a valid do not resuscitate (DNR) order in his chart. He is now refusing oral intake, and his daughter asks the team, "Since he's DNR, does that mean we can't consider IV antibiotics or a feeding tube anymore?"
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: "Yes — a DNR order means no further medical interventions of any kind can be offered."
"A DNR order only limits medications, so intubation and feeding tubes are still fully available if you want them."
"A DNR order prohibits cardiopulmonary resuscitation only; other life-sustaining measures, such as antibiotics or a feeding tube, may still be considered."
"A DNR order prohibits all invasive procedures, so we would treat his pneumonia only with oral medications."
"A DNR order automatically transfers all medical decisions to the family, since the patient can no longer express his wishes."

explanation_correct: A DNR order prohibits cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) only. The patient may still consider other life-sustaining measures, such as intubation, feeding tube placement, or chemotherapy. The team should therefore clarify that IV antibiotics and a feeding tube remain options to be discussed according to the patient's values and goals. DNR status does not curtail any interventions other than resuscitation from cardiac arrest.

explanation_incorrect.A: This dramatically overstates the scope of DNR, which addresses only resuscitation and not the many other medical decisions that remain open.
explanation_incorrect.B: This understates the scope in the opposite direction: DNR limits CPR specifically, not medications in general.
explanation_incorrect.D: DNR does not prohibit invasive procedures broadly; feeding tubes and intubation, for example, may still be considered.
explanation_incorrect.E: DNR does not transfer decision-making authority to the family; decisions continue to follow the patient's known wishes or the appropriate surrogate process.

educationalObjective: A DNR order prohibits CPR only; other life-sustaining measures may still be considered.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 59-year-old woman has recently been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and wants to plan ahead for future medical decisions while she still has full capacity. She asks the physician which legal instrument would give her the greatest flexibility in covering unforeseen clinical situations and allow her to name someone she trusts to speak for her.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation by the physician?

options.text: An oral advance directive, because spoken instructions are easier to update than any written document.
A medical power of attorney, because the patient designates an agent to make medical decisions and it is more flexible than a living will.
A living will, because it is the most flexible option and allows an agent to interpret the patient's wishes.
A do not resuscitate order, because it provides the broadest control over future interventions.
No document is needed, because her family is legally required to make decisions that match her current preferences.

explanation_correct: A medical power of attorney allows the patient to designate an agent to make medical decisions if she loses decision-making capacity, and she may also specify decisions in particular clinical situations. First Aid describes it as more flexible than a living will and revocable by the patient while capacity is intact. For a progressive disease like ALS with many unforeseeable decisions, this is the instrument that best meets her goals. Advance directive details vary by state law.

explanation_incorrect.A: Oral directives are the least reliable form, with problems arising from variance in interpretation, and do not designate a decision-making agent.
explanation_incorrect.C: A living will delineates specific interventions the patient anticipates accepting or rejecting and does not itself designate an agent; it is less flexible than a medical power of attorney.
explanation_incorrect.D: A DNR order addresses only CPR and provides no mechanism for a designated agent to make broader decisions.
explanation_incorrect.E: Without an advance directive, surrogate decision-makers must guess at the patient's wishes; preparing a document while capacity is intact is exactly the appropriate step.

educationalObjective: A medical power of attorney designates an agent, is revocable while capacity is intact, and is more flexible than a living will.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 70-year-old man suffers a massive stroke and can no longer make his own medical decisions. He never completed a written advance directive. His son insists that his father repeatedly told him he would never want to be placed on a ventilator, while his daughter recalls only one brief comment made years ago and argues it should not guide care now.
question: Which of the following factors would make the patient's oral advance directive more valid?

options.text: That the son is the eldest child and therefore has the strongest legal claim to interpret the patient's wishes.
That the daughter agrees to defer to her brother in order to avoid a prolonged family conflict.
That the statement was made to a physician in a hospital, since only statements made in medical settings count.
That the family votes on what the patient would have wanted and follows the majority opinion.
That the patient was informed when he made the statement, the directive was specific, and he repeated the same choice over time to multiple people.

explanation_correct: An incapacitated patient's prior oral statements are commonly used as a guide, but problems arise from variance in interpretation. The oral directive is more valid if the patient was informed, the directive was specific, the patient made a choice, and the decision was repeated over time to multiple people. These features make the repeated, specific refusal of ventilation the stronger guide for the team. Birth order, family consensus, and setting of the statement do not affect validity.

explanation_incorrect.A: Birth order does not confer legal authority to interpret wishes; validity depends on the characteristics of the statements themselves.
explanation_incorrect.B: Family agreement may ease communication but does not make an oral directive more valid or more faithful to the patient's wishes.
explanation_incorrect.C: There is no requirement that oral statements be made in a medical setting; repetition over time to multiple people is what strengthens them.
explanation_incorrect.D: A family vote reflects the relatives' preferences, not evidence of what the patient actually communicated while capacitated.

educationalObjective: An oral advance directive is more valid when the patient was informed, the statement was specific, and the choice was repeated over time to multiple people.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 65-year-old man with early-stage colon cancer designated his adult daughter as his medical power of attorney 2 years ago. Following a falling-out, he tells his physician that he no longer wants his daughter making decisions for him and asks to designate his son instead. He is alert, oriented, and fully able to discuss his diagnosis and treatment plan.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician?

options.text: Honor the request and document the change, because a medical power of attorney can be revoked by the patient as long as decision-making capacity is intact.
Explain that the designation is irrevocable once signed and must remain in place through his cancer treatment.
Tell him that only a judge can revoke a medical power of attorney once it has been executed.
Require the daughter's written agreement before any change to the designation can take effect.
Continue to treat the daughter as the agent, because the original designation controls even if the patient later changes his mind.

explanation_correct: A medical power of attorney is an advance directive in which the patient designates an agent to make medical decisions if the patient loses decision-making capacity. The patient may also specify decisions in clinical situations, and the designation can be revoked by the patient if decision-making capacity is intact. This capacitated patient may therefore revoke the daughter's designation and appoint his son. The physician should document the change according to state law.

explanation_incorrect.B: Unlike some irrevocable legal instruments, a medical power of attorney remains under the patient's control and can be revoked while capacity is intact.
explanation_incorrect.C: No judicial action is required; revocation of one's own medical power of attorney is the patient's right while capacitated.
explanation_incorrect.D: The designated agent has no authority over the patient's choice of agent; the patient alone may revoke and redesignate.
explanation_incorrect.E: Continuing to recognize the daughter as agent after a capacitated revocation would override the patient's autonomous instruction.

educationalObjective: A medical power of attorney may be revoked by the patient whenever decision-making capacity is intact.
source: Generated from 6. PHS.pdf - Ethics: Advance directives and DNR

subject: PHS
vignette: A 72-year-old woman completed a written advance directive 3 years ago stating that if she were ever in an irreversible coma, she would refuse mechanical ventilation and artificial nutrition. She now presents in a persistent vegetative state after a hypoxic injury with no possibility of recovery, as confirmed by two neurologists. Her son, who is at the bedside, asks the team to intubate her and start tube feeds despite the document.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician?

options.text: Intubate the patient and start tube feeds, because a written directive cannot anticipate her current clinical situation.
Intubate the patient but withhold tube feeds, since ventilation is the more reversible intervention.
Follow the son's wishes, because family members override written advance directives whenever they are present.
Follow the written living will and do not intubate or place a feeding tube, because it delineates the specific interventions she anticipated accepting or rejecting.
Request a court order before withdrawing any care, because written directives apply only while the patient is terminally ill with cancer.

explanation_correct: A written advance directive delineates specific healthcare interventions that the patient anticipates accepting or rejecting during treatment for a critical or life-threatening illness; a living will is the example in First Aid. The patient's documented refusal of mechanical ventilation and artificial nutrition in an irreversible coma applies precisely to her current condition. The physician should honor the directive rather than the son's contrary request. Details of such directives vary by state law.

explanation_incorrect.A: The directive expressly anticipated this situation — irreversible coma — so it directly governs the current decision rather than being inapplicable.
explanation_incorrect.B: Reversibility is not the criterion; the directive refuses both interventions under these circumstances.
explanation_incorrect.C: A valid written directive made while capacitated takes precedence over a family member's contrary preference.
explanation_incorrect.E: No court order is required to honor a valid living will, and such directives are not limited to cancer or any particular diagnosis.

educationalObjective: A living will delineates specific interventions a patient anticipates accepting or rejecting and is honored when those circumstances arise.
